analysis.one_liner: Requires SEC whistleblowers to report fraud to their employers first and makes whistleblower awards optional.
analysis.headline: A House subcommittee approved the bill 19-14 in December 2011, but the full House never voted on it and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the whistleblower program created by the 2010 Dodd-Frank law, which pays people who report securities and commodities fraud to the SEC. Under this bill, an employee would first have to report the misconduct to their own employer, then go to the SEC within 180 days, or lose any chance at an award. It would also make awards optional rather than mandatory, cut compliance officers out of the program, let companies fire whistleblowers for violating company policies without that counting as retaliation, and require the SEC to warn a company before bringing an enforcement case based on one of its employees' tips.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and executives facing potential securities or commodities fraud allegations gain the most. They would get first crack at investigating employee reports before regulators see them, advance notice before the SEC moves against them, a path to self-reporting credit that can reduce penalties, and a clearer ability to discipline whistleblowers under company rules. The SEC whistleblower program's deterrent power over firms would shrink.

how_it_helps.text: Employees would have to report misconduct to their employer before going to the SEC, so the company learns of the problem first and can investigate, remediate, and shape the record before regulators arrive; awards would be denied unless the employer lacked an anti-retaliation policy or anonymous reporting system, or the SEC found internal reporting wasn't viable.

The SEC would have to notify a company before starting an enforcement action based on a whistleblower's tip, and if the company responded in good faith it would be treated as having self-reported — a status that generally earns reduced penalties.
Awards would become discretionary instead of mandatory and the minimum-award formula would be repealed, letting the SEC pay nothing in any case and removing firms' uncertainty about large payouts.

Companies could enforce employment agreements, workplace policies, and codes of conduct against a whistleblower, and adverse action taken under them would not count as retaliation — weakening the anti-retaliation shield the 2010 law created.

analysis.who_pays: Whistleblowers and ordinary investors. Employees reporting fraud would risk exposure and retaliation by tipping off their employer first, and could lose awards outright under the compliance-officer exclusion, the culpability exclusion, or the 180-day deadline. Investors and pension savers would bear the cost of fraud that goes undetected because fewer insiders would risk coming forward and the SEC would learn about misconduct later, if at all.

drawbacks.text: An internal-first rule can be a trap for the employee: the person who exposes misconduct by or with the knowledge of senior management may simply be fired, and even where exceptions exist, the whistleblower must persuade the SEC within a 30-day preliminary review that internal reporting wasn't a viable option.

Requiring advance notice to the company before an enforcement action gives the very firm under investigation time to prepare its defense or settle privately, which could compromise cases built on a whistleblower's confidential information.

Making awards discretionary and repealing minimums removes the financial incentive Congress built in 2010, which the program's defenders credited with drawing high-quality tips from insiders who would otherwise stay silent.

The bill's strongest good-faith argument — that direct-to-SEC awards bypass companies' own compliance systems and discourage internal reporting — addresses a real concern, but the bill went further than fixing that, letting employers punish whistleblowers under company policies and warning them before enforcement.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered companies real protection: early notice, a chance to self-report, and less exposure to large awards. But the costs fell on the people the 2010 program was designed to protect — insiders who witness fraud — and ultimately on the investors who depend on insider tips to surface misconduct. The internal-reporting goal could have been pursued without the employer-notification and policy-enforcement provisions, which tilted the bill heavily toward the companies being policed.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared a House subcommittee in December 2011, but the full Financial Services Committee never voted on it, so it never reached the House floor and died when the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Michael Grimm introduced the bill on July 11, 2011, joined by original cosponsors Reps. Garrett, Stivers, and Campbell; it went to the Financial Services and Agriculture Committees.
The Capital Markets subcommittee had held hearings on the subject before the bill was introduced, and it was referred to subcommittees in July and August 2011.
On December 14, 2011, the Subcommittee on Capital Markets and Government Sponsored Enterprises marked up the bill and forwarded an amended version to the full committee by a vote of 19 to 14.
No further action followed: the full Financial Services Committee never voted, the House never debated it, and the bill expired with the 112th Congress on January 3, 2013.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Whistleblowers and the investors who rely on their tips came out ahead, because the Dodd-Frank award program stayed intact. The financial firms that would have gained advance notice of enforcement and a weaker anti-retaliation shield did not get it.

for.name: Rep. Scott Garrett
for.role: Chair, Subcommittee on Capital Markets and Government Sponsored Enterprises
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; chaired the December 14, 2011 subcommittee markup that forwarded the amended bill to full committee 19-14.

for.name: Reps. Stivers and Campbell
for.what_they_did: Joined Grimm in introducing the bill.

for.name: Five House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, all of them Republicans.

against.name: 14 members of the Capital Markets subcommittee
against.what_they_did: Voted against forwarding the bill at the December 14, 2011 markup, 19-14.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a full committee vote after the subcommittee forwarded it; the bill sat from December 2011 until the Congress ended.

against.name: Securities and Exchange Commission and whistleblower advocates
against.what_they_did: Opposed proposals to require whistleblowers to report internally before going to the SEC, arguing the mandate exposes insiders to retaliation and deters tips.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was Republican, and the December 2011 subcommittee vote of 19-14 matched the panel's partisan split, though the record does not list how each member voted.

industries.note: The bill would have given these firms first notice of employee fraud reports, advance warning before SEC enforcement, self-reporting credit for good-faith responses, and room to discipline whistleblowers under company policies. Its gain came directly from weakening the insider-reporting channel that surfaces fraud affecting investors.

The bill would have channeled reports through internal compliance systems, enlarging their role, but it also would have cut compliance officers themselves out of whistleblower awards when acting on reports received in their duties.
